subject: Post-call: NovaHealth performance / SLA probing — p95/p99 targets & throughput
messages:
From: Anna Morales <anna@novahealth.io>
To: camila_reyes@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Cc: Tim Baker <tim.baker@novahealth.io>
Date: Wed, 14 Jan 2026 16:12:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Intro + perf topics we promised to share

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier — helpful to see Redwood’s routing and fallback ideas. As promised, attaching a small anonymized traffic sample so you can sanity check the p95/p99 numbers we mentioned. A couple of clarifications from our side that came up after the call:

- Our peak traffic window is 11:00–15:00 PT, roughly 20% of daily volume.
- Typical request sizes: 95% of requests have <400 tokens input, but prompts can spike to 1k during complex summarizations.
- We have a strict SLA with our clinicians team: p95 end-to-end (client -> model -> client) must be <= 220ms for simple requests and <= 420ms for the heavier summarize calls. p99 currently tolerated up to 1.2s for heavy calls, but that’s causing user friction.

We’re open to a POC but need a concrete test plan: traffic shaping, payload mix, and measurement hooks (trace ids, time breakdown). Can your SREs consume the CSV and propose a test profile?

Best,
Anna
Anna Morales
Head of Platform Integrations
NovaHealth

Attachment: nova-traffic-sample.csv (CSV, 14 KB)

From: camila_reyes@redwood.ai
To: Anna Morales <anna@novahealth.io>, Tim Baker <tim.baker@novahealth.io>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 15 Jan 2026 09:03:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: sample + next steps (p95/p99 probing)

Anna — thanks for the traffic sample and the SLA numbers, this is exactly what we needed. Quick top-level response and suggested next steps from Redwood: 

1) Measurement approach: we’ll run a controlled POC against a hosted Redwood endpoint with two traffic profiles:
   - Baseline profile (80% simple, 20% heavy) to validate p95 under normal load.
   - Peak-window profile (simulate the 11–15 PT burst with 2x concurrency and 20% heavy requests) to evaluate p99 tail behavior.

2) Observability hooks: we’ll require X-Trace-ID forwarded in requests (we’ll echo back timing breakouts: ingress queuing, model token-stream, egress) so you can join traces with your front-end timings.

3) Acceptance criteria:
   - Simple requests: p95 <= 220ms, p99 <= 380ms;
   - Heavy summarizations: p95 <= 420ms, p99 <= 1.0s;
   - Throughput: sustain your baseline QPS with <=10% token-cost delta vs incumbents.

Ben and Marissa are looping in perf engineering to draft the exact traffic shaper and expected connection params (keep-alive, chunking for streaming). Marissa — can you take the CSV and sketch the 2 traffic profiles and a tentative runbook?

Time-wise: we can kick a 48-hour POC as early as next week if that works for NovaHealth. If you want, we can also include an autoscale stress stage to show graceful degradation/fallbacks.

Thanks — Camila
Camila Reyes
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference

From: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
To: Anna Morales <anna@novahealth.io>, camila_reyes@redwood.ai
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 16 Jan 2026 10:28:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: NovaHealth performance / SLA probing — draft profiles

Anna / Camila — I pulled the CSV and sketched two profiles (attached as 'redwood-p95-projection.xlsx') with concrete qps/concurrency values. Key assumptions and ask from NovaHealth engineering: 

- Assumptions from CSV: baseline QPS ~ 95 req/s; peak window QPS ~ 220 req/s (burst to 300 req/s for short intervals). Average token output per request for heavy flows ~ 450 tokens.
- Proposed POC plan (48 hours):
   * Day 0: baseline run (24 hours) — steady-state at baseline QPS to measure p95/p99 for simple/heavy mix.
   * Day 1: peak simulation (12 hours) — ramp to peak window profile and hold; include a 1-hour 'stress spike' to 300 req/s.
   * Day 1: graceful degradation test (6 hours) — introduce network perturbations and failover to fallback model variant to validate continuity.

Measurement specifics we’ll produce in the runbook: per-request timestamps (client-rcv, ingress-accept, model-start, model-end, stream-end), token counts, and CPU/GPU utilization samples. We will also compute delta vs your client-measured latency to ensure alignment.

Two clarifying asks for NovaHealth to confirm:
1) Can you expose the client-side trace ids in the sample rows (a column)? If not, we’ll map deterministic sample ids.
2) Are you comfortable with a hosted endpoint for the POC (no PHI will be sent; data ephemeral), or do you require a VPC Private test?

If both answers are yes, I’ll schedule the POC and send the runbook and a DocuSign NDA addendum (standard test terms).

Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood-p95-projection.xlsx (XLSX, 24 KB)

From: Tim Baker <tim.baker@novahealth.io>
To: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, camila_reyes@redwood.ai
Cc: Anna Morales <anna@novahealth.io>, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 20 Jan 2026 09:03:00 -08:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: NovaHealth performance / SLA probing — confirm POC scope

Thanks Marissa — this looks good. Quick answers to the two asks and a small tweak request: 

1) Trace ids: we can add a trace_id column to the sample CSV and will regenerate a slightly larger sample (attached) with a representative spike pattern.
2) Hosted endpoint: for the POC we’re fine with hosted as long as data is ephemeral and logs are TTL’d to 24 hours. We’ll still require a signed test addendum.

Tweak: can you add a token-limited run (cap output tokens at 512) in the heavy profile so we can see tail differences when the model emits shorter responses?

If you can update the runbook and send the test addendum, we can pick a start date (we prefer 01/27).

—Tim
Tim Baker
Principal Engineer, Platform
NovaHealth

Attachment: nova-traffic-sample-withtraces.csv (CSV, 28 KB)
